My SO and I speak 6 languages each, our 2 and 4 year old children speak 2 languages, with a few words or sentences from a third and a forth, AMA!
Thanks for taking the time to come here and do this! I was curious how you acquire such a variety of languages. Was it something you set out to learn or did you grow up in a variety of places?

It wasn't a goal or anything. I spoke 3 languages when I met my SO. She was raised bilingual because her parents are from two different countries, and then went on to study translation and languages. It so happens that I didn't speak any of the two languages of her family, so I started to learn them. Then I took pleasure and interest in languages, so I set out to learn my 6th language. I believe we transmitted our interest for languages to our children by our behavior, not so much with an agenda.

Awesome. I only speak 1 language and I'm jealous of you multi-lingual folks. I recall an exchange student in high school telling me the most difficult transition, for her, was that although she fluently spoke English she still thought in her native language. Is that equally true for you?

No, not anymore, although it invariably happens until some point for anyone learning foreign languages. At one point, you start to think in the foreign language and can drop the intermediate language (your native one). The more ability you have in your second language, and then the more experience you have in foreign languages in general, the less it is a problem.

To give you an example, I would watch movies in two or three different languages (I tend to whatch all my movies in their original language, with subtitles if I don't speak the language), and then a few days after, I can quote them in any of those three languages, without remembering in what language I actually saw the movie. The translation is made in my sub conscience, without even me realizing it.
What languages do you speak? Which ones do you children know?

I speak (Canadian) French as my native language, English, Spanish, Italian, German and I started to learn Esperanto not too long ago.

Our children speak French and Italian in equal measure and some phrases of English, with a song or two in German.

Our Neighbor is Colombian, I don't know if my children will pick up Spanish through the contact with his... Time will tell.
that's impressive! what are the 6 languages? and how do you teach your children the languages?

French, English, Spanish, Italian, German and Esperanto. My SO speaks Dutch, but not Esperanto.

For the moment, we don't really teach them languages, in the traditional sense. We barely talk to them in French and Italian, and make them watch some children shows in English (in addition to French and Italian). We also read to them in all three, and sing some German songs with them.

wow that sounds like a lot of work!

It's not much work at all, actually. Don't tell me any parent wouldn't make their children watch children shows, sing to them and read to them. The only difference with us is sometimes we choose shows, books and CDs in other languages.

Do we have disagreement? No. It never even crossed my mind that there could be. Maybe if I didn't speak her native language or vice versa, it could have been an issue, but the way it is now, no, not at all. As I said, we don't teach them, we simply talk to them like any parent would, in the languages we're most comfortable speaking. The languages that they ended up speaking are simply the ones we spoke to them in.

What languages do you speak? I'm attempting to learn Japanese right now, and it's quite challenging. What advice would you give to someone learning a language like Japanese (with different characters other than roman letters)?

I've already (just now) answered for the languages that I speak : French, English, Spanish, Italian, German and Esperanto.

I don't currently speak any language that doesn't use the Latin alphabet, although it's on my bucket list : I'd like to know Russian, Japanese and Greek, but I'm trying to strengthen the ones I know first. That being said, take my advice (at least for non-Latin character languages) with a grain of salt.

With the experience that I have with languages, I figured people put a lot of emphasis on the wrong things, and then they get discouraged and quit. Here's what people without much language learning experience tend to do : they learn a lot of vocabulary by heart, while concentrating on their spelling, and take forever before they actually try to speak with natives. They also don't put much (or enough) effort on grammar.

Here's what I recommend to do instead : think how infants learn their native language, they first learn to produce random sounds that are present in the language(s) of their parents, then they learn to speak, and then they learn to write and spell properly. Should you do exactly as children do? No. But nothing prevents you from taking the best approach by combining what's most effective in how adults and children learn.

So in your case, I would concentrate first on learning the letters of the three Japanese alphabets (maybe concentrate on one first, and then move on on the other two, leaving the Kanji for last), but specifically the sound each letter makes, so you know how to pronounce much of what you read, even if you don't understand what it means. Then, move on to simple phrases and get a feel of how to form sentences in Japanese. Concentrate on grammar and culture of Japan, the vocabulary you get from context will stick, the one you get from drilling by heart will not only be harder to remember, but the process will be uselessly painful as well. Notice how easy it is to look up a word in the dictionary, but you simply can't check a grammar rule or learn how to pronounce words on the fly while you speak to someone! Then, as soon as you can say "Hello! My name is /u/MarineByeologist. I'm sorry, I don't speak Japanese well. How do you say X in Japanese?", find someone, either in real life or online, to practice speaking with. It may take a while to find someone you enjoy speaking with, and who's patient enough to guide you through your learning, but don't despair. You should be able to learn much faster if you enjoy it, and you won't even notice how much new vocabulary you get (and remember) by speaking with people (or in mangas, or in movies, whatever), instead of drilling it.

This is my advise, it may not work for you. If you prefer drilling, learning things by heart, and are too shy to speak with anyone, then simply don't follow my advise. You'd better learn in a way that makes you comfortable than follow the best advise of an internet stranger and then quit because you didn't enjoy yourself enough (or at all).

Edit : About that language partner you could find to practise speaking Japanese with, try not to speak a single word of English with them, even if it seems to take forever to look up words in dictionaries and you make horrendous sentences, it's still the best way to learn. And if the language partner you find wants you to help them learn English, separate the sessions in Japanese and the ones in English so you don't get confused and revert back to English, and then never speak Japanese again out of laziness.
